newsitem.title: USA: NATO expansion to cost U.S. $200 million a year.
newsitem.headline: NATO expansion to cost U.S. $200 million a year.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Wednesday said NATO expansion will cost U.S. taxpayers about $200 million a year and predicted Americans will understand and support the cost of protecting U.S. interests in Europe.

In an interview with NBC's "Today" programme, Albright said: "The price is going to be about $200 million a year for us ... we believe it is not a price that is too high to pay for security. I have no doubts about the fact that the American people will understand this."

Albright also said that despite the price, Americans will endorse the expansion of the Western alliance as an alternative to war, saying, "the point here is that we do not want to have American men and women go and fight in Europe, and the way we're going to make sure that doesn't happen is through a reinvigorated and enlarged NATO."

The secretary's comments came one day after the 16-member group expanded by three to include Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- the largest enlargement in NATO's 48-year history. The move came during the second day of a NATO gathering in Madrid, Spain.
Albright said NATO, created to deal with threats from communist countries, now faced a new round of issues, including ethnic strife, border disputes and narcotics.

"Those are the kinds of threats that the American people and the international community is going to be facing, and if NATO had not adapted in this particular way (by expanding) it would not be doing the job that we need it to do to protect American security."

Russia, which is not a full-fledged member of the alliance, strongly opposed the expansion. When asked by NBC why Moscow was not included as a member, Albright said: "What we have said is that NATO will be open to every democratic government ... so ultimately it is open to Russia if Russia wants to join."

Russian President Boris Yeltsin chose not to attend the summit. His signing of a landmark treaty in May paved the way for enlargement while giving Moscow a voice -- but not a veto -- in alliance affairs.
The deal must still be approved by the U.S. Senate, and Defence Secretary William Cohen, interviewed on the same NBC programme, predicted it would.
"I believe the Senate ultimately is going to ratify this," he said.
